title: OET Reading Part A Practice
note: Unofficial self-study. Matching / scanning style drills.

sets.title: Acute pancreatitis — quick scan
sets.instruction: Four short texts (A–D). Match each question to the text that contains the information. One text may be used more than once.

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Presentation
texts.body: Patients typically report sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, often with nausea and vomiting. Pain may improve when leaning forward. Ileus and low-grade fever can appear within hours.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Initial investigations
texts.body: Diagnosis is supported by lipase (or amylase) at least three times the upper limit of normal plus compatible imaging when needed. Ultrasound looks for gallstones; CT is reserved for uncertain cases or suspected necrosis after 72 hours.

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Early management
texts.body: Aggressive but guided fluid resuscitation, early oral intake when tolerated, and analgesia are priorities. Routine antibiotics are not indicated for sterile inflammation. Gallstone pancreatitis needs timely biliary evaluation.

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Complications to watch
texts.body: Hypovolaemia, acute kidney injury, pleural effusion, and infected necrosis are key risks. Persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours marks severe disease. Nutrition support should not be delayed if oral intake fails.

questions.stem: Which text discusses when CT imaging is usually considered?
questions.explain: Text B: CT reserved for uncertain cases or suspected necrosis after 72 hours.

questions.stem: Which text mentions pain that may ease when leaning forward?
questions.explain: Text A presentation: pain may improve when leaning forward.

questions.stem: Which text advises against routine antibiotics for sterile inflammation?
questions.explain: Text C early management: routine antibiotics not indicated for sterile inflammation.

questions.stem: Which text links persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours with severe disease?
questions.explain: Text D complications: persistent organ failure >48h marks severe disease.

questions.stem: Which text refers to ultrasound for gallstones?
questions.explain: Text B: ultrasound looks for gallstones.

questions.stem: Which text prioritises early oral intake when tolerated?
questions.explain: Text C: early oral intake when tolerated.

gist: Scan headings first, then hunt for unique markers (timeframes, exclusions).
Part A rewards precise location, not outside knowledge.

sets.title: Community-acquired pneumonia — scan drill
sets.instruction: Match each item to Text A–D.

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Who needs admission?
texts.body: Use clinical judgment plus severity tools (e.g. CURB-65). Hypoxia, inability to take oral therapy, social isolation, and significant comorbidity often tip decisions toward inpatient care even when scores are borderline.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Microbiology clues
texts.body: Most cases remain culture-negative. Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigens help in severe disease. Viral PCR panels are increasingly used in winter peaks; a positive viral result does not always exclude bacterial co-infection.

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Antibiotic choices
texts.body: Start promptly after cultures if these will not delay therapy. Local resistance patterns guide first-line agents. Switch from IV to oral when vital signs stabilise and gut absorption is reliable.

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Safety-net advice
texts.body: Advise return if breathing worsens, confusion appears, or fever persists beyond expected course. Smoking cessation support and vaccine review belong in recovery planning, not only acute treatment.

questions.stem: Which text warns that a viral PCR positive result may not exclude bacterial co-infection?
Which text discusses IV-to-oral switch criteria?
questions.explain: Text C: switch IV to oral when vitals stabilise and absorption reliable.

questions.stem: Which text includes smoking cessation and vaccines in recovery planning?
Which text says most cases remain culture-negative?
questions.explain: Text B: most cases remain culture-negative.

questions.stem: Which text notes hypoxia as a reason for admission even with borderline scores?
questions.explain: Text A: hypoxia and other factors tip toward inpatient care.

gist: Look for tool names, exclusions, and decision thresholds.
